utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Witness. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Sir, I would like to inform you on behalf of this Chamber that you will be testifying with the benefit of pseudonym, which is KDZ-051, and image distortion. And this means that there will be no reference to your real name or information that may reveal your identity to the public or media. The audiovisual record of your testimony, which is broadcast to the public, will have a distorted image like this, which you can see in front of you. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This is to ensure that your identity is protected. And the transcript, while available to the public, will always refer to your pseudonym. I hope you are happy with this regime.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And during the course of your testimony, please don't hesitate to let us know if you need a break at any moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will begin by showing to the witness a pseudonym sheet. Can we have in e-court 65 ter 90280 and, please, not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, looking at the monitor in front of you, I would ask you to tell us, with "yes" or "no," whether you see your name.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this pseudonym sheet into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3403 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I would ask that 65 ter 90281 be uploaded in both languages and not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, is it correct that you provided statements to the Office of the Prosecutor and you also testified before this Tribunal on 31st March and 1st April, 2005, in the case of Momcilo Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review an amalgamated statement which contains portions of your previous testimony and your statements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes. I've reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Looking at the monitor in front of you, is this the first page of the amalgamated statement that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, it is the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Did you make a few minor corrections which were incorporated in this statement and then signed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Do you confirm that the statement is accurate, truthful, and if asked questions about the same subjects here in court, would you provide the same information?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this amalgamated statement under seal. Public redacted version of the statement is uploaded in e-court as 65 ter 90281A, and I tender it as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Both will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the unredacted statement will be Exhibit P3404 under seal, and the public redacted version will be P3405.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll read now a brief summary. The witness is a Bosnian Muslim from Rogatica. The witness knew Rajko Kusic as a friend and colleague for a number of years before the war. In April 1992, Kusic told the witness that he and the JNA had to defend the Serbian people and Serbian land. Around 22nd May, 1992, the shelling of Rogatica began. From a vantage point, the witness observed that Muslim-populated areas were targeted. After the shelling, announcements were made to the Muslim population to surrender to Serb authorities in the Veljko Vlahovic school. The witness, his family, and about 300 other Muslims were forced to go to the school in June 1992. Many new detainees arrived and the school eventually held about 1100 people. The witness was detained in the school for three and a half months. The school was guarded by Serb soldiers and police. Detainees were not provided with sufficient food or water. Many were subjected to torture, forced labour, rape, and sexual assaults. Among the rape and sexual assaults victims were minors. A number of people were taken outside the school and were never seen again. Occasionally shots were heard outside the school. At the school, guards forced detainees to sign papers stating that they had voluntarily joined the Serbian Orthodox religion. The witness was taken out of the school compound to see Rajko Kusic for interrogation. Kusic visited the school on about 10 to 15 occasions. During one of these visits, the witness heard Kusic say that he needed to report to Pale on the progress of cleansing of Rogatica. Your Honours, this concludes my summary, and I have a few additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, during the proofing on Sunday, did I play to you an audio recording of an intercept telephone conversation? Mr. Witness, did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So did I play to you an audio recording of a telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And were you able to recognise voices of the participants?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Who did you recognise them to be?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I recognised the voice of Mr. Radovan Karadzic and Mr. Sveto Veselinovic, although I'm not absolutely certain about Sveto Veselinovic's voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And how did you recognise the voices?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Well, I recognised the timbre of the voice, the topic that they were discussing. And in the case of Sveto Veselinovic, there is a high probability that that is indeed him because in one of the conversations he mentioned Rajko Kusic, so that made me pretty certain that that is him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we have in e-court 65 ter 30254, which is an intercept between Radovan Karadzic and Sveto dated 20 September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in front of you is a transcript of the audio recording of the intercept that you listened to on Sunday. At page 3 in English and page 4 in B/C/S, there's a reference to Kusic, and you already told us that based on this content of the conversation you believe it's Rajko Kusic; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And why do you believe that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Well, because in the context of their conversation there was mention made of Rogatica and Kusic. And knowing that Rajko Kusic at the time was an organiser and commander of the Chetnik unit at Borike, as it was referred to by both Serbs and Muslims at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this intercept to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P3406, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in your statement you said that Tomo Batinic was the president of the Municipal Assembly. Can you clarify: What assembly were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Tomislav Batinic was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Rogatica, but he was in fact the president of one of its parts, the Serb part of the town of Rogatica. In other words, Mr. Batinic was the president of the Municipal Assembly of the Serbian Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 07160. First page of this document is a cover letter sent from the Rogatica Executive Committee to the RS Ministry of Defence providing them with a report on the work of Municipal Assembly from July 1992 to September 1993. Could we have e-court page 8 in English and e-court page 6 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 in English, and it's 3 in B/C/S, it says, on 26 December 1991, Tomislav Batinic was elected president of the Municipal Assembly. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Is this the same person you talk about in your statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we please have e-court page 5 in English and e-court page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Here it talks about the establishment of the Serb Municipal Assembly, and if you look bottom of the page as well as next page in B/C/S, which is e-court page 6 and 7 in English, there is a list of deputies of the initial Serb Municipal Assembly, and the first person on the list is Tomislav Batinic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now I want you to go through this list of names and indicate persons you knew personally, and please tell us if you would like us to go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel kindly switch off his microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at this point, there is no need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this list I recognise Tomislav Batinic, Predrag Malovic's name, Gordan Vucak, Rajko Kusic, Vlastimir Lelek, Milanko Lelek, Radoje Popovic, Slavko Lubarda, Veljko Bojovic, Milorad Sokolovic, Drago Vukasinovic, Milorad Jagodic, Vojko Ujic, Boban Jesic, Miroslav Obradovic, and Slobodan Puhalac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know whether they were members of any political party?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: As far as I know, most of them were, or, rather, I believe that all of them were members of the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And among these people, who did you see visiting the Veljko Vlahovic school during your detention?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Do you mean from this list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, among these people that you -- yes. And if you want to see the page before, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Could I please see the previous page once again. Looking at both sides, both pages, and the names on both pages of this list, Tomislav Batinic came to the Veljko Vlahovic school, Rajko Kusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I offer this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3407, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in your statement, you said that Rajko Kusic was member of the SDS and you also said that he was your friend before the war. My question to you is: Do you know where in Rogatica, what part of town or neighbourhood, was he living?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: The house of Rajko Kusic was on the outskirts of the town, in Karanfil Mahala, in the Karanfil Mahala neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And do you recall the name of the main street that was running through that area?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: That was Titova Ulica, which ran from the southern part of the town all the way north towards the road for Sarajevo. And on the left-hand side, this neighbourhood was, and Rajko Kusic's house in it, in Karanfil Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 18176. This is a list of the SDS Main Board members with addresses and telephone numbers. And I would like to have B/C/S last page, and in English second-last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So now, if you look top of the page in B/C/S and in English just below middle of the page, there is a name of Rajko Kusic, his address, and telephone number. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It says here that Rajko Kusic address is Titova Street. Does this correspond with your memory whether this was home address?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 18176 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it Titova or Tita Street?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, if you see in English it's already translated as Marsala Tita. And in B/C/S it just has this, at the end it changes the letter. Depends how you call it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3408, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now I would like to show a short videoclip. Could we have 65 ter 45262A. This is an ITN report about Rogatica, one year after the fighting started. I would like to play a very short portion of it. And if you can play it when it's ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this person we see on this frame, who -- do you know who the person is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: That is Tomislav Batinic, Tomo, president of the Municipal Assembly of the Serbian Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And Batinic says here: "Serbs and Muslims cannot live together and the Serbs want their own state once for all." Mr. Witness, is this consistent with statements made by SDS officials that you had discussions with including Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The phrase, the words you cited, is the words of this Mr. Batinic or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Mr. Batinic said these words on the tape, on this videoclip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the transcript says, "the Serbian mayor of Rogatica told me that ..." We didn't hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So what we have here, narrative, is speaking what mayor of Rogatica told him. But in background one, if listen to this, can hear really what Batinic says, maybe not the whole, this line or sentence, but portions, yes, definitely. What we have translated here, what narrator said, not what Tomislav Batinic said. But he's quoting Tomislav Batinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there a way that we reflect the -- what is said in the transcript? We didn't have the sound, i.e., English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I also didn't hear sound. Maybe we can play it once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it that the transcript was offered to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Actually we didn't offer because one sentence, and they can read, but I agree with you I also didn't hear the words. I propose we play again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot interpret when there are several interpretations going on at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I suggest we play it once more and then it will be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Serbian original cannot be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we are not sure who it is that said this phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: What we can try, Your Honours, is to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can ask the witness whether he could hear what Mr. Batinic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Maybe this clip is not set up in the way that witness can hear that, but what we can do is try to translate each words, who said what, because we have one original B/C/S; then we have, in English, narrator speaking; and then there is this TV in Belgrade, they then translate what was said in English. So it's a little bit -- I agree with you it's a little bit confusing, but we can try to make transcript to reflect words of each these persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And we can offer to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we don't object to the admission. And it will be for the weight as to who said what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You do not object to it on the ground of the third party's statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I asked the question to Mr. Robinson, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because this appears to be a contemporaneous statement, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the journalist was a witness here, so why was this not tendered through him? We cannot discern what was taken out of context, out of what Mr. Batinic had said. The journalist was a witness here. Why wasn't this dealt with through him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That cannot be a reason to preclude from -- preclude the Prosecution from tendering the document. We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3409.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that there is that constraint, namely that it should be established first who was saying what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take the words that Prosecution will do that exercise in due course. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We will. Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Witness, this is my final question to you. I would like you to tell to the Court in your own words how the experience you survived have impacted you and your close family members.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: All of these things that happened from May 1992 and onwards left a profound effect on me and my family and friends who managed to survive. Rogatica was a small town full of understanding, full of life, with lots of mixed marriages between Muslims and Serbs, between Serbs and Croats, between Muslims and Croats. Rogatica was a town where one could have a good life, where we all had jobs, children went to school. There was a great deal of scenic beauty there and we all enjoyed it. We celebrated Christmas together with the Serbs. We celebrated Muslim holidays together and Catholic holidays together. This really all contributed to this wonderful image of a small town in Bosnia which, in May 1992, ground to a halt, in blood at that, by the so-called Serb army, by the Chetniks of Rajko Kusic, who relentlessly fired at the town from the hills around it for months, thus victimising the population. Most of them were Muslims, because our Serb neighbours had moved out. Sometime in May, Serb children, mothers, the elderly were moved out somewhere. Later on we found out that they had moved out to Serbia. And then that relentless shelling started, day after day, when children and old people were being killed, houses destroyed. After three or perhaps even three and a half months, the Chetnik forces and the forces of the Serb army entered town, cleansing it, without selecting the means they used to do so. Regardless of whether this had to do with children, the helpless, the ill, they killed them or they --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I don't -- I apologise. I don't want you to go -- this is in your statement. It's already in evidence. I want you just to tell us how this all impacted you and your family. Very briefly. But you don't have to go through all of these details because it's all in your statement. Can you tell us, just briefly, what -- how it impacted you and your family.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I do apologise. My answer seems to have gone the other way. But it's hard to avoid not saying all of this. My family went through a terrible experience. At that time in 1992, my daughter, who was 7 and a half, was raped, several times at that. My son, who was 13 years old, was raped for months. And that is what is the most painful of all. They raped me too, but I somehow survived that. But it's hard in the case of one's children. I cannot -- I cannot get rid of those images. I cannot free myself of these thoughts that this was done by my former friends, my neighbours. I know all of these people who committed these crimes against my family. And I find that very hard to take. As for all these difficulties that my family had, for all of three and a half months at the school, and for about ten months in this other part of town, all of that left a lasting imprint on my psyche. I have been under treatment for the past 16 years. I'm so ill. And I'm trying to forget at least part of it, but I don't seem to be able to. I've never asked my wife whether she had been raped too. I don't have the strength to do that. But I assume I don't have the right to ask that either. She was taken out as well, but we never discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just looking at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's appropriate to take a break now. We will break for 20 minutes. --- Break taken at 9.42 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, Judge Baird will say a few words to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Witness, are you now composed or do you want us to give you some more time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber is not unmindful of the distress you are experiencing as you deliver your evidence. And we want to let you know that if at any time or at any stage of your evidence you think that you might need a little break to compose yourself, do let us know immediately, and we will rise and accommodate you. This is very important. If at any stage of your evidence you think you might need some time just to settle yourself, let us know. We will rise and accommodate you, and it does not matter how often you make that request. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Karadzic starts his cross-examination, we need to deal with associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. There are six associated exhibits, one of which is already in evidence. That is 65 ter 07330, now P03291. One exhibit should be under seal, 65 ter 07880.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The remaining five items will be admitted and given number in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please do accept my sympathies and solidarity for the pain you've experienced, and do help us try to shed light on what happened exactly and who did what in Rogatica. Today, on page 8 you said that Kusic lived on the outskirts of Karanfil Mahala. What was the majority population in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the majority population was Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Rogatica, there were areas that were predominantly Muslim or predominantly Serb, even 100 per cent, but there were these neighbourhoods, the Carsija?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, an integral part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that within the inner city itself there is not more than one kilometre, I mean the diameter is not more than one kilometre?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I assume that there is more, not a lot more, perhaps one kilometre, 200 metres, but roughly that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, on page 13, you spoke about how beautiful life in Rogatica was. Do we agree that you are speaking about Rogatica at the time when Rogatica and Bosnia-Herzegovina were in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: In that period, and also after the disintegration of Yugoslavia, we in Rogatica, since Bosnia got the status of a republic, it became independent, we in Rogatica lived a normal life. We worked, we went out to taverns together. Actually, in my view, life in Rogatica changed after the disintegration of Yugoslavia in the sense of, well, we got a new name, but basically life in the company where I worked, in the cafes and taverns that I went out in, didn't change much, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So these six weeks from the 6th of April until the 22nd of May were as if there wasn't any war going on in Sarajevo, Kupres, et cetera; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: That's how we felt in Rogatica. I had occasion to sit and talk to my Serb friends about that, and we all hoped for a long time that in Rogatica there would be absolutely no problems. I, personally, as I talked to people I had that impression, that after all in Rogatica, Visegrad would not happen, or any of the other things that happened in some other places in the beginning, because Rogatica is a small town that lived a life of its own. And actually, that's how I felt, at least. I had no reason to believe that something major would happen in Rogatica. I personally trusted my Serb friends a great deal. And if there would be any problems whatsoever, or any military interventions, my street, which is a very small street that is adjacent to a street where the population was 100 per cent Serb, whereas in my street, it was 100 per cent Muslim, and we got along very well. Sometime towards the end of April there were talks and contacts between us to the effect that even if there were to be any military things going on, the Serbs in Donje Polje, that's the name of the street near the church, they were saying that they would be willing to protect us, from my street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to get to that. You also say at one point that they asked you to come and seek shelter with them when there is fighting.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, but not when there was fighting. It was in this peacetime, if there were to be any kind of conflict or any kind of intervention, that we could rely on them, that we could come to Donje Polje and we would be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 7 today, you expressed your opinion or, rather, your conviction that most of the members of that - now, was it the Crisis Staff or the Serb Assembly of Rogatica? - were members of the SDS. Do you remember who the president of the Crisis Staff was of the Serb Municipality of Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I think it was Sveto Veselinovic who was president of the Crisis Staff. Actually, as for that information, I had not received it officially from anyone because I did not hold any official position in town. So it wasn't that SDS or SDA people would be in contact with me. I was just a normal citizen who tried to the very end to live there. And through this co-existence I found out that Sveto Veselinovic was president of the Crisis Staff of the Serb part of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that a witness confirmed here that that was a different name and that that man had been a communist, that he was not in the SDS, but all right. We will deal with that with someone else. You said that elections were held, that the SDA had won, that the Serbs came second, and the third was the SDP. Do we agree that in the SDP there were both Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer to that question, frankly speaking, because I'm not aware of the situation. I don't really know how many people were in that political party. But I assume, on the basis of the private conversations I had with people in Rogatica, that there were some Serbs there too, specifically a few persons. I remember that well now. The director of Tehnotrans, for instance, Rade -- basically the last time we walked through Titova Street was when we walked together, only the two of us. It was Rade Jovicic. And Rade said to me -- although I never asked him, actually, which party he was in. I wasn't really interested in that. But he said, We both made a mistake for not having gone to these political parties, you to that Muslim party and me joined the SDS, in order to prevent the kind of problems that were already happening in Visegrad and Foca and elsewhere. I can also say that in the SDP there were Serbs and Muslims, but I don't know what the actual numbers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the participants, let us explain this. Do we agree that the SDP actually succeeded the League of Communists of Bosnia-Herzegovina but they just changed their name?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer to that question. Frankly speaking, I don't know. I did not know very much about the League of Communists of Yugoslavia or the SDP or any other political party. I wasn't interested in that. I was a man who was a sportsman, who had practically dedicated his entire life to sports, not politics in any way. So for me to say that the SDP was succeeding the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, I really cannot say. I don't know. I was not interested in that before, and I'm not interested in that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the president of the Crisis Staff could have been Milorad Sokolovic and that he was not from the SDS?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I really cannot say. I repeat: My knowledge of politics and my political information is very scant. I really cannot tell you whether Milorad Milo Sokolovic was president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps the Trial Chamber and the participants are going to find this to be of interest. Do we agree that this Milorad Sokolovic is from the same family like Mehmed Pasa Sokolovic, the grand vizier of the Ottoman Empire, perhaps the most successful grand vizier in the Ottoman Empire, and that Mehmed Pasa is from your area?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I really don't know. I have not heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's difficult to see the point of your question after having heard the witness's answer that he didn't know Mr. Sokolovic. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I wanted the Trial Chamber and the participants to learn a bit more about us. This Mehmed Pasa built the bridge on the Drina, and it is world renowned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not giving evidence here today. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm referring to paragraph 7. It seems that you talked to Mr. Kusic quite a bit when the conflict broke out. And you say there that Rajko Kusic said to you, Radovan is paying me better. Are you sure that that is what Kusic said to you, and do you know that our soldiers received a monthly salary of five marks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know about the salaries, how big they were, but that is true, what Rajko said to me. We were together in the same company, and when he left the company I asked him why he did that, because we were good friends, and he smiled and said, Radovan is paying me better. I didn't ask him anything else about that. I mean, we did continue talking, and then I asked, How are you going to live now since you're not going to be working in the company? And he said that he would open a privately owned shop, that he would be involved in trade a bit. I saw Rajko later on in the marketplace. He was selling -- selling brandy, grape brandy. I seem to remember that detail very well. And I walked up to him and we exchanged a few words and I asked him how business was going on he said, Fine. And that was that. That was that conversation. And that is my answer to your question in terms of what Rajko had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we are not going to deal with this, but do you actually believe that the entire finance of the SDS was under control and the SDS did not pay anyone except for five or six employees?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Believe me, I never sought this information and never heard of any such thing. I wasn't really interested. Even when I talked to Rajko, I did not have an opportunity of hearing anything. Quite simply, this was not my line of work, politics, finance, whatever, anything that had to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that in the tensions between the civilian authorities and the military Mr. Kusic sided with the military?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not quite understand your question. Can you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in Republika Srpska there were tensions between the civilian authorities and the army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: In Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Republika Srpska. Between the Serb army and the Serb authorities, that there were misunderstandings and tensions.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Which period are you referring to? It's not clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. That was later on during the course of the war. Never mind. You said in the same paragraph that Serbs received severance pay in order to leave their jobs of their own volition. Are you referring to socially owned enterprises or private enterprises?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I'm referring to socially owned companies because I know that some of my friends in the company where we worked together received the severance pay and left the company and they probably wanted to go into private business or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned here who did what. Do we agree that government was divided between the Serbs and Muslims on the basis of the agreement reached between the SDA and the SDS at republican level, and the president of the municipality was Adil Lutvic, a Muslim; the president of the Executive Board was Mile Ujic, a Serb; the chief of the public security station was Ismet Omanovic, a Muslim; the commander of the station was Mladen Vasiljevic, a Serb; the commander of the Territorial Defence, Mehmed Agic, a Muslim. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Quite frankly, you know more than I do. Quite frankly, I was not involved in any of this. I did not go into that, who was doing what. I always looked at people individually. Were there more Muslims in the Municipal Assembly or in the police or whatever, I was not interested in that. Absolutely not. I always had good relations with all people. And for me, that didn't really matter, who held which particular position. Perhaps I was disappointed that this or that person held a particular position and in my view he was not really up to it, but now that is my own affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You speak about certain things about divisions in the municipality and in the police, and you even say here that this division in the police was ordered, that is paragraph 9, ordered by Sveto Veselinovic, Mladen, and Rajko Kusic, and so on. So I have to ask you this: Were you familiar with the negotiations that were underway in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the negotiations aimed at Bosnia's independence and Serbs accepting that? Were you aware of the Lisbon Conference, the plans that were discussed before the conflict broke out and during the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No, sir. As for this scant information that I had, I got it from people that I took walks with and that I met up with in cafes. It was just briefly that I'd hear this information, the news from our town, political news from our town. And that's how I received this information, for instance, that one day people who were in the police and who were ethnic Serbs had separated and went to Karanfil Mahala and then the other police remained there. All of this was the information that I had from my fellow citizens there. It wasn't on the radio or in the newspapers. I simply did not look at that in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these talks about dividing the municipality and dividing the police station into two different police forces followed from the Lisbon Conference and the Cutileiro Plan? You didn't know that, did you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 10 you say there was no active army in town but everyone was on the reserve force and that you, too, were summoned to drills before and after the elections. Before the elections, did you respond to these call-ups, and how long did the drills last?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes. I was part of a reserve unit that belonged to our company. And I believe in those years, after I returned to Rogatica, in those five, six years, I participated in the roll-call in the compound of the factory where I worked, and once at the stadium where there was a large number of us during that roll-call that lasted two or three hours, but we did not have any activities. At least I was not part of any activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was a reserve unit of the JNA that had been established within your company; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was established just in case, in case of war. Do you know that some other reserve units went to training grounds and training centres, camp training, for several days, for exercises?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: It was only by chance that I heard that some military exercises had been carried out, some war games, involving only Serb reservists. And if I remember well now, there was a line-up at the sports centre. We were told that Muslims need not respond to call-ups anymore, those call-ups to the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. But I'm asking before the elections, before the crisis. Do you remember that some men went for several days to camps and military exercises and came back home with uniforms and some also with weapons? Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions, again, unofficially, I would be told by someone that a group of Serbs had armed themselves and brought weapons home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. I'm now talking about the time before the elections and before the crisis. But let's discuss what you just mentioned. Are you saying that you were told that Muslims were not needed anymore, either their officers or their troops? You say that in paragraph 10, that they were not needed anymore or their Muslim army. What did you mean, what kind of Muslim army, Muslim troops?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I meant the Muslim men who were part of the reserve force, that unit in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do we agree that Rogatica was in the area of responsibility of the 216th JNA Brigade whose command post was in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, or that location. I was never interested in that sort of thing, and I never heard anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the man number 1 in that brigade, Chief of Staff, until and even after the outbreak of the conflict was Asim Dzambasovic, now a brigadier of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that Asim Dzambasovic has to be a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I suppose so, by the name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, on this point I'm slightly confused, Witness. Did you know that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, after the outbreak of the conflict in Slovenia and Croatia, the Muslim and Croat part of the Presidency recommended to Croats and Muslims not to respond to JNA call-ups either into the reserve force or the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that from some municipalities, such as Vlasenica, even if reservists did go to Banja Luka they went in an organised way and brought back Muslims on buses?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it ever announced in the media that the JNA was renouncing on Muslims, reservists and conscripts?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you learned that somebody from the JNA said that, was any explanation given, why Muslim reservists, officers, and recruits were not needed in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: On that day, no explanation was given. Later on, people talked among themselves, but I was not interested in those stories and I didn't want to get involved at all in any way. The first vibes I got that somebody was -- something was about to happen in that state of ours came only later, but I never got any information that could constitute an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 11, you say that most members of the SDS were seeing people from the JNA and that the JNA had meetings with prominent Chetniks and that Chetniks wielded great influence among the Serbs. Can we make it clear: What do you understand by "Chetnik"? Do you mean people who are fond of Chetnik symbols and who call themselves Chetniks, or all Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No, not all Serbs. Just those who joined those Chetnik detachments, such as Rajko Kusic. I don't know how all that was organised, nor was I interested, but I know they did organise themselves into a group. And, of course, not all Serbs in Rogatica joined the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that from the beginning until the end, by 20th May, this detachment commanded by Rajko Kusic was a legal battalion of the 216 Brigade of the JNA and later grew into a brigade of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to Rajko Kusic, were there any Chetniks, as you call them? You mentioned the skull-and-bone symbol and cockades.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: When do you mean? Before the war or after the war started?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At any time.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: There were such people, and I specifically saw a couple of men I knew who were wearing those emblems, and I was frightened, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 12, you describe that one day a large number of officers and troops came to the municipality and they had come to collect the weapons that lay in depots for Territorial Defence. You say that the Muslims resisted, there was shooting, some Muslims were wounded by JNA soldiers, et cetera. Now, let me ask you: Do you know that the weapons of the Territorial Defence were stored in JNA barracks in 1990? That's before the elections, and it was during the communist regime.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this visit by the JNA to your municipality followed an incident when a small group of JNA officers was told they could not collect documentation from a military department in one locality and then they showed up in larger numbers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Muslim side removed that documentation and the JNA never received it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it is impossible to carry out mobilisation without that documentation except by going from house to house to see whether there are any reservists and whether anyone would respond to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you were present at this incident and you observed this clash. Do you know that the JNA was entitled to all military structures including documentation, and it was prevented from exercising its constitutional role?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm saying that again. I had absolutely no interest in these things. At that time I was present, it was purely by chance, because (redacted) If you think that I wanted to be there, no, it wasn't like that. I just happened to be there. And I described the whole thing in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at page 28, at line 22, I ask it to be redacted, the name of the street. Also reference to family member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think almost everyone in (redacted) (redacted) so it's not an identifying detail. But I don't mind the redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking this because that features in your statement, and the defence has to test the basis of your knowledge and your position, because maybe it would have been better if they had limited you only to things that you personally experienced and saw. But this is also a good answer, that you noticed these things by chance without knowing any context or background.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You know -- you say in paragraph 13 that Serb men were at their military positions outside Rogatica, whereas Serb children and women had already left, leaving in Rogatica only Muslims and a few Serbs who did not see eye to eye with Kusic. Now, tell me, is it true that before the outbreak of the conflict a large number of both Muslims and Serbs left Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes. Although, as far as "large" in your sentence is concerned, I don't know because I was there and I could see how many Muslims were left in town when the shelling had already begun. And I can say again, with great certainty, that a large number of Serbs had already been evacuated, whereas some Muslims had been moved out of Rogatica in an organised way, although I don't know who organised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are talking about the time before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in your assessment or to the best of your knowledge, what were these people running from, both Muslims and Serbs? What kind of feeling did they have that made them think it would be better to seek a safer place?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that Muslims were afraid, afraid of something that would not be good. And as far as I know anything about my Serb friends who left, they may have known or felt that war was afoot. In any case, a large number of my friends moved out, moved to Serbia, with their families. Not only Serbia; some moved to Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But would you allow the possibility that they, too, were afraid?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Nobody leaves their home easily. It must be some kind of fear, fear of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that on the 22nd of May the conflict broke out and there was shelling. Do you know and do you agree that there was an incident which contributed to a significant increase in tensions, this was in March, where -- involving some Muslim barricades followed by some Serb barricades? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 23rd of March Muslims erected barricades and then on 24th of March the Serbs did too, and then Colonel Milosevic arrived there and he exerted his influence so that the barricades were removed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Well, I don't know any details, but I do know that both sides erected barricades depending on where they lived. As for the street where I lived, we did not erect any barricades. We had coffee together, we socialised, we worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now briefly take a look at P2371 in e-court to help you refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, 3271, P3271. Yes. Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the date on top. That's the 24th of March. And then it goes on to say that on the 23rd, Muslims set up barricades, that this hampered the operation of the economy and schools, and then on the 24th of March the Serbs built up their own barricades. And then Nermin, from SUP, he was the one who sent this. Do you know who this man was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do know who Mile Ujic was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, we went to school together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at the addressees of this communication. It was addressed to the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then to the Government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To the Ministry of National Defence and the Ministry of the Interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If this was not corrected, there was a misinterpretation of -- of the SRBH, where reference was made to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas it should be Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, in e-court that was marked erroneously, but now we see that it says Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because it says that Rogatica is in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And we had an abbreviation for this which was SRBH Presidency. So can we please have that corrected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, after this incident, this was -- the problem was defused. There was no conflict as a result. And there was a lull for another two months, right, until 22 May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes. At the time that you mention, there were no problems, at least I didn't have any problems. I went to work regularly. I didn't see any barricades on either side. And even if there were any, I didn't go to those areas because I wasn't really interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that an agreement was reached to have two municipalities and that the Serb local communes were to be under the Serb administration, whereas Muslim communes were to be under Muslim administration, and the municipal building itself was divided so that half of it was used by the Serb Republic -- by the Serb Municipality of Rogatica, and the other one by the Muslim municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Well, yes, I know that it did happen. But what was under whose authority, I don't know, and I didn't even care.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you are an artist of sorts. I understand that you now engage in art of sorts.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Well, yes. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 13 that there were killings of Muslims near Rogatica and that this caused panic. Do you know this personally? Did you have occasion to see any of those killings?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, then, that on the 20th of May a Serb policeman was killed in the Serbian municipality -- local commune of Zlatni Do? He was on the beat, patrolling the area after the agreed separation of the police forces, and his body, they did not want to surrender his body. They said that they would surrender his body when ten Serb policemen have been killed. Did you know of this?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say here, in paragraph 14, that your knowledge derived from stories from people who lived in those villages and who saw a Serb soldier killing several people, including women. The people who stated that are Muslims. Could you please tell us the name of the village and of those people so that we can check your story without actually involving you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Well, I can't really recall this. I can't recall either the village or the people who told me about this. I didn't know these people. As it concerns this incident, what happened was that these people came from the village, from their village, and told these stories. They said that these were Chetniks who killed men, that there was a slaughter there, and that's about it. That's all I can say about this detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you talking about the period after the 22nd of May or before?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Before. Because before May 22nd I could move freely around town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 15 that you heard that a villager, a farmer, had been killed while he was gathering his cattle.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 16, you say that an elderly Croatian woman had fled from a shelled village and that she took refuge in your house, where she stayed for a while. How long did she stay at your place?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Two days and a night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What village had she come from?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know. I am from Rogatica, but I absolutely have no idea what the villages or hamlets around Rogatica were called. I just know the place where I had an aunt whom I visited from time to time. But as for all the other villages or hamlets, I really didn't know much about them nor did I have reason to have any knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the name of this Croatian woman?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I can't really remember. I just know that her husband's name was Jozo, that she was Croatian. I believe that her husband was a forest guard or ranger, and that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 18 you said that you saw soldiers coming on trucks, parking next to the culture centre, and unloading some crates that you assumed contained weapons, but you did not really see them.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, this new depot, the warehouse where one time -- which was one time a municipal hall or a centre, was that guarded by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Well, there were some people guarding those premises that I knew, but there were others whom I didn't know. So that I don't know if they were members of an army or what army or at what time, because there were all kinds of armies there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, they did this openly outside this community hall; right? There was nothing covert about it. They would just come there, unload the trucks, and that's how it happened; right? We saw this in paragraphs 18 through 21. If you have your statement before you, you can take a look.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you need it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. "These were military trucks that belonged to the JNA and trucks owned by my Serb neighbours who came near a church." You didn't see what was in them or on them but you concluded that this could have come -- that that these could have contained weapons. So did they use the community hall as a new arms depot? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Well, the only difference being that I didn't call that the community hall. We always used to call it the hall. This small building was always referred to as the hall. Now, this building housed for a while an orphanage right after the Second World War, and then for a while there were some other institutions there. But in any case I don't know if it was a community hall or whatever else it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. But I've read what you said in paragraph 18. "It parked near a community hall." That's what I quoted.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Well, that's probably how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that at this time the JNA was withdrawing from Slovenia and Croatia, that they were withdrawing and pulling out a lot of military equipment from those areas, and that they were withdrawing towards the Yugoslav border?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I didn't know that detail, nor did I care.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 23, you say that you did not know of any arming of Muslims in that area. Does that mean that you didn't know that there was the Patriotic League there, that there were Green Berets there, that there was a municipal headquarters under the direct control of General Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No, not in the context that you put it in. I'm not aware of that. It is true that I knew and heard the words "Green Berets" or "Chetniks" or "Uzice Corps." Somebody might have mentioned them, but I did not know anything about that, nor was I interested in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But did you learn later on whether the Muslim side in Rogatica was organised within the Patriotic League and the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know Hamid Bahto and have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it witness has said no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was to the question whether I knew Bahto.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was the previous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... to the question whether you learned later on whether Muslim side in Rogatica was organised within the Patriotic League and the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you didn't even learn about it later? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Not in the way you're asking, not in that context. I heard of those monikers, Patriotic League, Green Berets, and some corps, but nothing of that added up, because first of all I didn't care about these things, and, second, I was too small to do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And have you heard of Hamid Bahta [phoen], did you know him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Never heard of that name. I know of the surname Bahto because there are several people with that surname, but I did not know Hamid Bahta and never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 24, you stated that Kusic was based at Borike, that he was a commander -- the commander of a paramilitary unit, which did not come to Rogatica but underwent training in smaller villages, and they wore on their caps the skull-and-bone badge and insignia, including SDS letters. Is there any trace of those insignia? Are there any photographs? Have you ever seen any?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Never seen any photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we ask you that you draw, during the break, what that emblem on the cap looked like?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't think I could do that. It was a long time ago. Such a long time ago that when I -- but I remember seeing my friend Marinko with a cap that had the skull and bone on it and three letters, a smaller S, a bigger D, and again a smaller S. Perhaps I could make a sketch, but I'm afraid of not getting it right and then my answer would be seen as dubious, as well as your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Witness, that the position of the SDS was neither Chetniks nor partisans? Do you remember that we did not approve of any Chetnik iconography?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Didn't Kusic himself tell you that his unit belonged to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you have more for your cross-examination. If it is convenient, the Chamber will take a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. But from 110 I came to the 24th paragraph, and I wouldn't like to leave any of them unclarified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I would really need to go to the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will take a break for half an hour and resume at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. You have an hour to conclude your cross-examination, after which we will have a break for 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We left off at the point when I said that Rajko Kusic let you know that he and his group belonged to the legitimate JNA army. You thought they didn't. However, in paragraph 95, you say that when you asked him what was going on, his facial expression changed and he only told you that he and the JNA had to defend the Serbian people and Serbian lands; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph, you say that Gucevo village also had its own JNA unit, led by Radomir Bukva and Petar Jesic, so it was quite clear to you that these were reserve forces of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Until the 20th May, 1992, the JNA was a legitimate armed force, wasn't it? The only legitimate army in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I suppose that's correct. But I am not very conversant with the whole system, after the break-up of Yugoslavia, which army was in Slovenia, which in Croatia, which in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I didn't really care at the time, nor did I learn anything about who was officially in charge, where the army is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that war was going on already on 26th of March in Bosanski Brod, a little later in Bijeljina, 3 April in Kupres, and a bit later in Sarajevo? Did you know about these theatres of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina that spared you for six weeks? Did you learn about that from the media?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know, or perhaps you didn't know and I don't hold it against you, but maybe you knew that the SDA tried to trick us by reneging on the agreements that we had made in order to accept the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 32 and 33, you say, in paragraph 33, that you went to a neighbour's house. Was that a Muslim neighbour - I'm trying not to mention his name, look at paragraph 33 - and you stayed with him for 20 days?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, that's my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Don't tell the name.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: His house was across the road from mine. He had two floors, whereas my house was low-standing and already damaged by then. We moved to his place and found shelter from the shelling throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You anticipated my next question: What were you hiding from, from the police or from the shelling, and why was that house safer than yours? But you've answered. So that house was more solidly built, and you were hiding not from the police but from the shelling.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm a little nonplussed that you were able to see not only the place where the shells were fired but also the place where they were landing. You say, in paragraph 56, that a certain person - and you give us the name and surname - fired a shell which killed a boy.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the distance between the firing place and the landing place?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't really worried about the distance either then or now. If you're asking me to give you the precise distance, I can't. How much could it have been, as the crow flies? Maybe 150 metres, maybe 200. I can't tell exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of shell is fired at that distance? Is it a mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know what it's called. It's a tube attached to something. And you must understand I know strictly nothing about weapons, because I served in the army as a driving instructor and I only had infantry exercises for a month. I wasn't interested in weapons at all. It was a tube attached to a platform on the ground, and it was not a very long tube.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And at 150 metres it killed that boy?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I suppose it was 150 metres. I'm not claiming it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 36, didn't you say that the battles for the town itself, with the shelling and the conquest of houses one by one, the street fighting, lasted all in all two and a half months?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree, then, Witness, that it had to involve some resistance, because the whole length of that small town was 1.2 kilometres and you could have taken it in two or three hours, not two or three months?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: May I make my answer a bit more precise, if I take a bit more time. In all the conversations, when we were already at the camp, with my former friends and neighbours, I asked the same question, "Why didn't you come into Rogatica immediately?" Because in Rogatica, the town itself, there were two and a half thousand, 3.000 people, completely unarmed. Nobody had a weapon. There was no shooting from the town. Whereas over two or three months the helpless town was shelled constantly before they finally realised there was no resistance. And I said in my statement that I heard Rajko Kusic had received criticism from you why Rogatica had still not been taken, and then they finally came into the town, after so many months of completely unjustified shelling without any rhyme or reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll have to take it up with someone else, because it's so illogical that such a small town with a main street of 1.2 kilometres takes two or three months to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please refrain from making statements or comments, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask him if it sounds as illogical to him as it does to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether it was illogical or it was done by design, but the fact is that's the way it was done. And Rogatica town, which some people needed even later, was completely devastated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said two mosques had been destroyed, and I want to ask you if you know that one of them was restored with the help of the Government of Republika Srpska and the government of Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that the Catholic church, although there were very few Catholics, was left intact?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I agree, because I spent two or three months in the immediate vicinity of that church when military activity was already underway, and the Catholic church was perhaps riddled by a few bullets but not shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that perhaps you did not have good insight into combat operations and the war around Rogatica and that's why you think there was no combat?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: When I said there was no combat in Rogatica, I said it consciously. And leaving aside the fact that I don't know what was going on around Rogatica, but in Rogatica itself there was no shooting by Muslims, and there were no weapons in the hands of those Muslims who remained. They remained in the belief that their Serb neighbours would do them no harm. I was one of those who stayed in Rogatica. Both Serbs and Muslims suggested a few times that I should leave, after some other people had already left, but I always said, "I'm staying because I don't think anyone would do me any harm." In Rogatica there was no military activity, at least where I moved around, including the centre of the town and all these streets like mine, and the adjacent streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's not recorded in the transcript, your answer concerning paragraph 15, that you heard that a farmer who was grazing his cattle was killed. I asked you: Have you heard about a Serb farmer? The "Serb" was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that a shepherd was killed, a Serb. But how, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you say, in paragraph 39 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 08207. I'm not sure the Prosecution tendered this document, although you dealt with it. Could we see it again in e-court. I believe it can be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was one of the associated exhibits we admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's now Exhibit P3414, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that it was an associated exhibit, but I see that it hasn't been shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, would you please take a look at this regular operational report, and can you see that it says there that the requests are the same as the one sent on a daily basis? Now do you know that brigades addressed their superior commands and reported daily to their superior commands on their activities?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you commented on this document, in paragraph 39 of your statement, where you also say that you were civilians, there were no weapons there, that the weapons were held by Serbs. Now, please take a look at a couple of important issues here. In the first paragraph it says that Kusic is reporting to his superior command, the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Large numbers of Muslim civilians arrive in town every day, mostly women and children and unarmed people. The people are finding shelter in the secondary school centre. Is that secondary school centre the Veljko Vlahovic school?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: What it says in this report, that's one thing. But what I saw - and to me that is the only truth - is something quite different. According to this, a huge number of civilians -- well, in fact, the civilians did not come to the secondary school centre. Rather, they were taken there by Chetniks. They were brought there as war prisoners because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were there two secondary schools in Rogatica or just one?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: There was only one secondary school, but there was an elementary school, too, that was used to detain civilians as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the next paragraph. It says the snipers are firing from a couple of places in town. This is on the 11th of June. The enemies -- provoked by opening fire on a column moving in the direction of Gorazde. And then you can see that it goes on to say that parts of the brigades are still participating in actions in the town. And then it says we didn't have any losses, whereas the enemy had five soldiers -- five casualties, military casualties.
