And then it says the other units of the brigades are holding positions facing the enemy. And then it goes on to submit requests. It says how many bullets were expended, and so on. And then do you see that it says people from villages are moving to the town and they're being accommodated at this secondary school centre, snipers are active in the town, there is fighting in the town, there are various operations in town, whereas all units are deployed on various positions and they're exhausted? Are you saying that in Rogatica town, on the 11th of June, and around Rogatica there weren't any positions where the two opposing armies were facing each other off?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I can't really say that. All I'm saying is that this report does not reflect the truth as it was on that day. In the sense that I can explain, in any case. I can't -- as to what -- compared to what I know about -- in view of where I was, what I experienced and what I saw and heard. Now, the 11th of June, that's already the second or third day, which means -- of my detention at the camp, so I wouldn't have known anything about this. And all I could hear is this shelling, merciless shelling, of the town and the taking of prisoners for interrogation from the centre. As for this report, I can't really say anything about it, nor can I answer your question, because I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please take a look at 1D01113. 1D00013. 1D0113. Yes, we seem to have the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, please take a look at this. This is a bulletin of daily events put out by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska, and it says: In spite of the agreed cease-fire, Muslim extremists are taking offensive action in some parts of the territory, and so on. And then it says: In Rogatica itself, from Zivaljevici village, populated exclusively by Muslims, an attack with snipers and mortars was launched against the surrounding Serbian villages. This is on the 6th of May, or St. George's Day. Now, would you agree that Zivaljevici is a Muslim village, and did you know of this attack?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't know that Zivaljevici is a Muslim village. And number two, I didn't know anything about this attack. As I've already said, I didn't know much about the villages or any war or pre-war operations there. I didn't know much about it, nor was I interested in that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document and this is in relation to what the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Based on the answer of the witness, I don't see basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, could you help us in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we can try this with another witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we take a quick look at D572.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the second paragraph, where it says that in the general area of Rogatica there is an organised daily -- there are organised daily attacks by the enemy and they are repelled with arms, but we are having great difficulty at this because our brigade is deployed and -- is deployed and its ranks are thin because of the length of the front line. Now, did you know that this brigade, the Kusic brigade, was stretched out over a large front line and that it had great difficulty in repelling enemy attacks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far are Medjedja and Ustipraca from Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Ustipraca is about 20 to 25 kilometres away, whereas Medjedja is a bit further off, maybe some 30 kilometres or so, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know which army was employed in Medjedja and Ustipraca at the time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that it was the Muslim army and that they were deployed there for a long time, could you accept that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No. I don't know why that would be of any concern to me now and why I should find it acceptable or not. I don't know anything about this report. I don't know anything about the situation. And I can't draw any conclusions based on your guidance, and I cannot accept them. I think that it's absurd -- it's even absurd to discuss this document with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wouldn't do that, trust me, but the Prosecution actually asked you to comment on combat reports, and they submitted, tendered, combat reports through your testimony. So I just wanted to examine what you knew about it.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I really would appreciate it if you refrain from offending me. I was never instructed as to how I should reply to questions or how -- what I should say, and I am here as a human being, as are you. I bear you no grudges. I don't hate you. I came here to tell about the horror that I went through, the three months of shelling while I was in my house. I went through the hell of the camp and the 17 months of abuse by Serb soldiers and Serb police and Chetnik volunteer forces from Serbia. So, please, do not burden me and accuse me of being guided or taught or coached by someone as to what I'm going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I do have to clarify some of the paragraphs of this statement that was drafted by the Prosecution. And in paragraph 36, it says that there was no resistance of any kind. And then you were shown a report by Mr. Kusic to his commander. Witness, sir, did you ever see a report that Mr. Kusic sent to me?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: It was never shown to me. He never showed it to me. But I believe that in the Krajisnik case I did -- I was shown some documents. I did have occasion to see some documents, but I can't really tell now what they were. I just know that in a conversation with me, in several conversations with me, Rajko Kusic said that he had to report to Pale and to you and to the military leadership of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You served in the army. Was Kusic a captain of the army at the time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. We all had to address him at the camp as "Vojvoda." What his rank was in the army, I don't know. Sometime later, maybe in 1993, I learned from some Serb friends that he had the rank of either captain or major. I'm not sure anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Probably toward the end of the war he had the rank of major. Now, you served in the army. Can you agree that a captain or a major, a colonel, or even a general, would not send his reports to the president of the state but, rather, to their immediate superior officer, to their immediate superior officer? Is that the principle that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Well, in the JNA that's how it was. And what you're saying is quite acceptable. There was a chain of command. Now, what it was like in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war, within the VRS, and in view of all the paramilitary units there, who commanded whom, that's hard to tell. And I don't know anything about that, nor am I interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 34 you say that you saw Arkan's units, that you learned that they were deployed or stationed at Borike, and that in Mesici you saw the 5th Uzice Corps. Did you see the Uzice Corps yourself, and when was this, if that was the case? You say it was in mid-July; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I said that it was the Uzice Corps. And from everything that we learnt at the camp, that we could learn at the camp, from my acquaintances who were Serbs, it is possible that it was the Uzice Corps. And from the school building itself I did see columns of military vehicles with troops and weapons. I saw this myself, as well as did many other people who were at the school. But also, to answer your question about Arkan's Men, I didn't see them at Borike because I couldn't go there, but I was told by Rajko Kusic himself, literally, that there were 300 Arkan's Men, the White Eagles, at Borike. And his demand was that I should try and ask the people who are being interrogated at the camp to tell the truth because if not then he would order the mobilisation or, rather, an action by those men from Borike.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear that, as it says here, the Serbs were told that they had to seek shelter, to move out and wait for -- until these events were completed, these activities?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Well, I heard the shelling went on for a couple of days and then there was -- there were some military vehicles that had loudspeakers and they were calling for Muslims to come out of their houses; if they had weapons, to surrender them; and then to report to the school. And that was the information that I learned. And although I was very scared, I and a few neighbours of mine finally decided that we should venture out and go to the main square where the school was and see there for ourselves what was going on and whether there was any development, any movement forward. And there, when I got there, in a very short time over 2.000 people, Muslims, who didn't have any weapons, so there was nothing to surrender to anyone, they gathered there. And then there was an armoured vehicle that arrived there, a self-propelled cannon or something. It came there, a man came out, he said that we should hand over our weapons, there was this announcement, and we were told that we should report to the security centres at the school building. Now, knowing where the building of the secondary school centre was and knowing what it looked like, I said that we couldn't all go there because it wasn't big enough to hold us all, that there was not enough room for all of us, that we couldn't stay there. What were we going to eat? Where were we going to cook our meals? What toilet facilities were we going to use? because there wasn't enough of that. And he said that we would just stay there for a couple of days and then be released home. And then we agreed with Zivojin to request from the military -- from the Serb military leadership and tell them that we, the 2.000 or so of us who were there, that we were prepared to accept the Serbs moving into town, for the police going back to their own duties, that the Serb flag could be hoisted, and we would recognise the Serb Republic if only they would stop shelling us so that we could continue our normal lives. And his reaction was that -- was that he just looked at the ground, he said that he sympathised with us and he would do his best to actually get that to happen. But he returned a few moments later, not long after that, and he said that that was impossible. He had received an order that all Muslims should be taken or driven to the secondary school centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You speak about that in paragraph 46 and the next few paragraphs, and you say that all of you were told to go to the secondary school centre for a few days.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But then you say that, further on, around 300 people were killed. Do you have information that 300 people were killed in that combat in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what day it was. I think it was 19 June. Yes, I think it was 19 June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your statement says July.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I was, at the time, at the secondary school centre, and at one point a soldier came in. I didn't know him. He had the Serbian traditional cap and the Chetnik sign on the cap. And he ganged up on me straight away, saying, It's you I was looking for. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: (redacted) and Gracanica and another place we killed 300 people within an hour, including children. We didn't care how old the children were. His eyes were bloodshot and he was a bit drunk. And I recognised his voice, and I was wondering, Is the bloodshed going to continue there in the camp? And he didn't stay long. He left very soon. So this information about 300 people killed came from Zeljko, that soldier who told me that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take care of it. Are you referring to line 3 and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. And a few lines up also the witness mentioned name but it's not in transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think the witness mentioned Gracanica, but I do see "Gracanica" in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... street. His neighbourhood. It was mentioned at page 54, line 3, but that was second time it was mentioned. One -- first time it's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You confirmed that you say that the civilians stayed at the high school centre for three and a half months; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Roughly that long, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you confirmed that the taking of Rogatica took three months; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So when the Serb army took Rogatica, then civilians were released, and some prisoners were sent to Rasadnik; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how was it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: After Rogatica was taken by the Serb army, and while the city was being taken over, many civilians from the high school were transported, several times, taken to certain places, and men were separated from women and children for these transports. They were taken in a different direction. Quite a few civilians went missing from the high school centre. Over night they were taken out for questioning, and later on they did not return. After the military operations in Rogatica were over, the civilians at the high school centre were yet again placed in different locations. I cannot say who was transported and where and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard of Asim Hodzic, an old Muslim general who was from Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I have heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was in constant communication with the Serb authorities and that his advice to five villages in the Rogatica area was to hand over their weapons and these villages were safe?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say that Tomislav Batinic was a moderate?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Before the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say that during the war, as well, he took humanitarian aid to a Muslim village and you thought that because of this help given to the Muslims he was replaced by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know about him being dismissed. But the brother of the killed soldier who was in the vehicle with Tomo told me everything, well, not everything, but he told me this story: Namely, on that day, when what happened, happened to Tomo, Tomislav Batinic and Radomir Cerovic were driving coffee, sugar, oil, flour to one of the villages in the direction of Sarajevo in order to have that distributed to the Muslim people who had stayed in their village. That happened two or three times. And Radomir Cerovic and Tomislav Batinic were cautioned. That's what the brother told me. Kusic warned them not to do that again, and if they tried to do it again, things would not be good. After they took this aid to people for one last time, on their way back they came across a land-mine. Cerovic was killed and Tomo was injured in the face and lost an eye. Now, was it because of that that he was dismissed or awarded, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that he was a candidate on the list of the SDS after the war and that he was president of the municipality for as long as he wanted even after the war, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I did hear that after the war he was president of the municipality too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, for example, that the villagers from Satorovici, Muslims, came to the high school when there would be fighting somewhere, they went home to bathe and to get food, and they would stop at the high school centre whenever they needed to do that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No. And that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. That is what a witness said here, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I'm not interested. I know that I was there and that that did not happen. No one dared leave the high school centre without having one of the Serb soldiers or paramilitaries take him out. Also no one could enter either, without Serb soldiers or paramilitaries doing it, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D4297 in e-court. Please take a look at this. Just a moment, please. Page 2. Can we have page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a statement given by another person. We are not going to tender it. Let's just see what this person says about this in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English it's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "In the period between June 8 through 24 July," do you see that? "... we had no problems --" let me just find it in Serbian. Can you find it in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I cannot find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 1 in Serbian. Maybe it's page 1 in Serbian. Here it is, yes, the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "In the period between the 8th of June through the 24th of July, we had no problems as far as I'm concerned, as well as my family. We were all together in a classroom. Every 15 days we were given small amounts of food. During that time, I was allowed to go home to get some food and clothing and the other prisoners were allowed the same, but only those who had lived in the vicinity of the school." And so on and so forth. Do you see that those who were brought in from somewhere else were allowed to go out and that that pertained to other persons, other prisoners, too?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No. No. This is the one and only case in which this lady had a privilege, under quotation marks, to be able to go to her apartment every now and then. But never on her own. Always accompanied by Kovacevic, a Serb soldier who had some kind of close relationship with her, and I never went into that. It is true that she lived with her family in a room. And that room was so small. So small. Between the classroom and the teacher's room, there was this room where teachers left their teaching aids. And it was about two metres wide and three metres long, perhaps, and that is where this family was, in that room. And it is true that every now and then she did get some food from Mr. Kovacevic who was a soldier who took care of her. For what reason, I don't know because I wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does she not say that this Kovacevic was a colleague of her husband's from work, and doesn't she say that this pertains to other families as well, not only her?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Only her. It is for her to say what she said, but I know what I know. I was in a room that was close to hers and I was there with my family, and 40 other persons, in the teachers' room. That's where we were staying. So every day, very often, we would meet in the hall. Sometimes we would exchange a word or two, but very seldom. She tried not to talk to us too much because practically every day she was visited by this Kovacevic or other soldiers, so I cannot go into any details in relation to her statement. I don't think that this pertains to all the families that were there, because other families did not enjoy such a privilege.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 67, did you say that questions were put to you about your ham radio station and about the members of your family who were in the Muslim army? Was that the basis for your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know. One day -- now that you've mentioned it, one day, two soldiers came. I did not know them. One of them called out my name, found me, and then he showed me a picture, a big picture, of high school students, a graduation photo, and he asked me what the name of one of these persons was, one of the teachers. As for these teachers from Rogatica, I didn't know very many of them because I spent a lot of time outside, out of Rogatica. I returned just on the eve of the war, so I didn't know these soldiers or, rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: -- these teachers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then he told me to tell the truth. He took me to the basement then, where I was beaten up. That interrogation was carried out by two people from Pancevo, Noka and Kosa. Those were their nicknames. I never found out what their names were. I didn't really express any interest, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What unit were there, the White Eagles, what?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know. Noka had a small red cap and a camouflage uniform, and the other one -- actually, he had civilian clothing on too. I know that he had trainers, jeans, and a military blouse, and he had a limp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say in paragraph 72 that one person was bragging as to how many persons they had raped; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you do not know what he did, you just heard what he said?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I said in my statement what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we move into closed session just for a minute, please. Actually, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 87 did you say that you had not seen any killings in camp, however you saw that they were taking certain people out, and then you would hear gunshots and these people would not come back; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Witness, in practically all testimonies this sentence is contained. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have any contact with anyone. For already 16 years I am basically a man who has to live his own life, and I try to, with my pictures. I'm not in contact with anyone and I'm not interested in anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also said that one person said, You don't need to take a coat, you won't be needing it. Right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that sentence is often repeated in the testimonies of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Probably. Because when that happened, I was directly at the door, when Ljubinac, that soldier, asked Mujo to go with him. But behind my back there were quite a few inmates, and people probably heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I'm not speaking about witnesses from Rogatica but from all locations. The same thing is repeated. They were taken out, gunshots were heard, they were not returned. So it seems -- so what do you have in common? Only the OTP.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Sir, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, all right. In open court, you spoke about torture and rapes. Who knew about that? Where was that happening, and who could see that and know of that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I think that the entire Serb police in Rogatica knew about that. The entire military command knew about that, of the Chetniks, and of the Serb army. Because, actually, many, many, many of them are participants in that. That did not have to be discussed and it wasn't discussed, that's my assumption, because everybody did that, or practically everybody. Three months is a long time. Three and a half months are a very long time. My greatest pain is that so many friends and acquaintances of mine unnecessarily tarnished their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were friends with Mr. Kusic. Did you tell him what was happening to you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity to do that because he avoided contacts with me when this physical mistreatment started. He avoided contact with me. We had contact in the beginning, twice, and once in a group, in the school. As for all his other visits, they did not include contacts with me. I was expecting this. I actually asked his driver, again, a good friend of mine, former friend, to arrange a meeting with him so that I could say a few words. However, he never responded. All of it was -- well, the man didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 90, do you say that you were three metres away from him when you heard him saying that he was delayed in his cleansing of Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said to us. There were about 200 of us in the classroom, because they were preparing some action and then they squeezed us all into a classroom. I don't know what was being done during that action. And then he came there and he lectured us briefly, all of us, in relation to our interrogations with the police or the army. I have to say that there were provocations, taunts, from his side, because at one moment he addressed me directly, very briefly, and he said that I should expect that too, that it's possible that my son, who was 13 at the time, would be mobilised and that he would defend Serbdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was a single Muslim mobilised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask Your Excellency to notify me in advance of the last ten minutes because then I would move on to some documents that I had not intended to present. This is really too little. There are 110 paragraphs. There is too little time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's why the Chamber allowed your Case Manager to be present at the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, the OTP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you inform anyone? And can you know with certainty that you had informed about -- any one of the Serbs about everything that had happened to you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity to inform anyone. There was one opportunity when Mr. Tomislav Batinic came to pay a visit to the camp. I tried to talk to him on that topic. He just lowered his head and briefly said to (redacted) it's too late. You'll all be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Secondly, is it correct that you were considered to be privileged by the Serbs and that many Muslims were jealous of you because of the treatment you enjoyed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know where you get that information from. When the entire family had been raped for three and a half months, suffering, rape, beatings, if that is a privilege, then whoever gave you this information, well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the witness's statement because a microphone was switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have these statements in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 64, line 8, there's a name the witness mentioned I ask to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4296, can we have that, please. I believe that this was admitted as 92 ter, or something was admitted under this name as 92 quater.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. In Rogatica --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please don't have this broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- with a privileged status, the following remained to live there. And then there's a name with a family, and then another name with a family. And then it says that the first person had a hernia and never left the house (redacted) moved about quite freely. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I did not have a hernia. My neighbours from Donje Polje, Fedjo Planincic [phoen], Nedo -- Nedovic Dank [phoen], rather, and Mackenzie - I cannot remember his real name now - beat me up so badly that I could not go out for work obligation. Instead of me, they took my son, my 13-year-old son. And he was building sniper nests in Rogatica, and he was burying corpses in Rogatica. And he did all the things he did. And then finally on that day he was even sexually mistreated. And my wife did not move about freely. My wife was escorted by Serb soldiers. She went to do some kind of work. What it was, I never wanted to ask her.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's page 65, line 6, the name should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zec. That was your last question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more document that corroborates this, please. The first statement was this statement of Alija Zivakovic [phoen], and I think it's 92 ter. That's how it was admitted. Some of the Alija Zivakovic documents were admitted under 92 ter. If not, I would like to have this page admitted. And if I have been given permission to go on, I would like to have 1D4295. Again, I don't want to have it broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be your last question, Mr. Karadzic. And as you may know well, there is no basis to admit the last statement by Fatima Jasenkovic [phoen]. We will not admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But let us just see page 5. Let us see what she says about this. Let me just put this to the witness. We don't have to have it admitted. Let it not be broadcast, though. 514 is the last ERN number. Can we see the ERN number, please. I have 08554 so then it's not the right number. Pasic, Miljho; a certain Zijko; Alija Isakovic; Nadelj Isakovic; Faruk Isakovic; Borovac; and so on, all of those who were loyal to the Serb authorities and therefore sheltered at the school centre. And your name is there, as well as the names of your family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you accused by the Muslims of having been privileged, of having enjoyed the favour of the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: No. Most of these Muslims knew. A vast majority of them knew. Because they were citizens of Rogatica, they knew that I was a great friend of Rajko's. Perhaps that is what led them to think something, but that's absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I don't have any time left, I have to say for the sake of the transcript that I regret not having more time to shed light on what the witness heard and what he actually saw directly and who knew about all of these things. This was not the right page. The ERN page I asked for is RR088514.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then it may be a wrong -- different document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the name was right. Jasenkovic, Fatima. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's for you to organise your defence. That's it, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Zec, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Only one brief point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, today, at page 44 of today's transcript, Dr. Karadzic talked to you that -- that one of the mosques in Rogatica was rebuilt by the help -- with the help of the RS government. That's line 6-8. And in line 9 of page 44, you said, "I know that." I want to know: Do you know the date when the mosque was rebuilt, or year, or anything?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: I don't know the date and year when it was rebuilt, but I'm not 100 per cent sure that this was done by the Government of Republika Srpska. As I've already said in my direct answer to this, I knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In your understanding was the mosque rebuilt during the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-051
utterances.text: Considerably after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness, sir. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of my colleagues, this Chamber, as well as the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it, notwithstanding all the difficult circumstances. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will take a break for 40 minutes. But before that there are two matters to deal with briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, with respect to your request for leave to reply in relation to videolink testimony: Given that the Chamber is well aware of the jurisprudence on that issue, the Chamber won't need the reply from the Prosecution. And finally, Mr. Robinson, in relation to your binding order motion with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina dated 31st of August, 2009, it's still pending before the Chamber. My understanding is that you had an interview with General Delic, Sead Delic, already, and so the Chamber would like to know if there is any further update on Brigadier Brdjanovic and also whether the interview that you conducted with General Delic will have any impact on your binding order motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. The interview with General Delic concludes the obligation of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina with respect to that binding order motion. With respect to Brigadier Brdjanovic, I have an appointment to meet him on Sunday, so I can advise the Chamber. If I'm able to meet him and complete that interview, then we can withdraw that binding order in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, can I just raise one other matter. And this is that we would ask that there be a reclassification of a closed -- of a private session testimony that occurred on the 19th of September during the testimony of KDZ-075. We ask that page 19055, line 23, to page 19058, line 19, be reclassified as public. And the Prosecution has advised us they don't have any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be done. That's granted. We will have a break for 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I always forget to mention: The audio/video part will be also published as well. We'll resume at ten to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of September, 2011, at 2.15 p.m. 25
